title: ⭐ Practice: naming what a mind can do

questions.prompt: Sonia is never still, she misses no training session at the club, and she says what she feels with her hands and her face. Which intelligence does she show?
questions.explanation: "physical intelligence" is the one: energy, sport and feelings carried by the body are its three signs, and Sonia has all three. "emotional intelligence" would show in the way she weighs on other people, "mechanical intelligence" in repairing an object, and "creative intelligence" in inventing something new. A gesture is none of those three.

questions.prompt: Nadia has played the oud since she was five, and nobody ever taught her. Which sentence describes that?

options.text: She is a real gift for music.
She has a gift for music.
She has a gifted for music.
She is a prodigy for music.

questions.explanation: "She has a gift for music." is correct: a gift is a natural ability, so it is something you have, and it takes the preposition for. "She is a real gift for music." turns the person into the ability. "She has a gifted for music." uses an adjective where a noun belongs, and "She is a prodigy for music." keeps the wrong preposition after a word that names a person.

questions.prompt: Which word names the organ inside your head that you think with?
questions.explanation: "the brain" is the organ itself, the part of the body the whole lesson is about. "the gift" is an ability that organ makes possible, not the organ. "the prodigy" is a young person, and "the curiosity" is a wish, so neither of them can sit inside a head.

questions.prompt: One line of the model poem is "Undertaking projects". What does undertake mean there?

options.text: to take a project away from a partner
to take something out from under a table
to work under the orders of somebody else in a firm
to begin a piece of work and take charge of it

questions.explanation: "to begin a piece of work and take charge of it" is the meaning: the pupil of the poem starts the project and carries it himself. "to take something out from under a table" and "to work under the orders of somebody else in a firm" both read the two halves of the word separately, which is the trap. "to take a project away from a partner" would need a verb of taking from, and the poem describes what a pupil does, not what he steals.

questions.prompt: Your partner reads your draft and writes: "You have used the same word four times; look for another one." Which of the three points is he correcting?
questions.explanation: "the vocabulary" is the point: a remark about which words you chose, and about repeating one of them, is a remark on your stock of words. "the grammar" would be about a wrong form, and "the ideas" about something you say or fail to say. "the spelling of the words" is not one of the three points the lesson asks a partner to look at.

questions.prompt: Complete: "Her memory for names is ___: she can greet every pupil of the school after one week."
questions.explanation: "remarkable" is right: the gap follows is and describes the memory, so an adjective is needed, and remarkable means so good that people notice it. "remarkably" is the adverb and would have to sit next to another adjective. "remark" and "remarked" belong to the verb to remark, which means to notice or to say, and neither can describe a memory.
